forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news.title: Green-led council plans to ban cooperation with Home Office on immigration raids
news.summary:
Exclusive: Lewisham council’s move marks first step in Greens’ plan to create a corridor of sanctuary boroughs across London

A Green-led London council is planning to ban its officials from working with the Home Office on immigration raids, after uncovering evidence suggesting government officials wanted to use environmental health data to target restaurant workers.

Councillors on the Lewisham borough council are due to vote next week on a motion that would review its systems with a view to ending any cooperation with the government’s attempts to deport people without the right

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham forecasts £10.0m overspend on high needs schools funding, taking cumulative deficit to £34.0m
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council expects to overspend by £10.0m this year on high needs funding (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities), according to the Period 4 financial monitoring report going to the Mayor and Cabinet on 7 October. That would take the council's dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) deficit to £34.0m by 31 March 2027, up from £24.4m a year earlier.

The report attributes the overspend to growth in the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans and to higher costs charged by providers. There are now 4,003 children with a plan, compared with 3,744 in July 2025, a rise of 259 over 12 months.

The council submitted a SEND Reform Plan to government, with a deadline of June 2026, and expects the outcome in autumn 2026. If the plan is successful, the report says, government funding of up to 90% of eligible deficit costs could be secured. If it is unsuccessful or unsupported, the deficit falls to the council within the statutory override (a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet), which has been extended to 31 March 2028.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham's capital spending surges 62% in three months, forcing major new borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Lewisham Council's four-year capital spending forecast jumped by £263m in three months, from £421m in March to £685m in June 2026, forcing the authority to shift from relying on its own cash reserves to active borrowing on the capital markets. The council will borrow £42m for general spending and £31m for housing in 2026–27 alone. The expansion, largely driven by the Building for Lewisham housing programme, comes as the council's liquid investment reserves have depleted by £54m in a year to £210m. Debt service costs are projected to rise from 4.8 per cent of the annual budget to 7.7 per cent by 2027–28, constraining spending flexibility. The council is borrowing at a time when interest rates remain stubbornly high: the Bank Rate is forecast to stay at 3.75 per cent or rise further, and long-term borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board costs 5.6 per cent over 25 years.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham cuts pension contributions as £301m surplus grows
news_drafts.lead: Lewisham Council's pension contribution rate fell from 21.5 per cent of payroll to 17.6 per cent from 1 April 2026, releasing money for other services. The reduction follows a sharp improvement in the fund's finances. The 2025 triennial valuation — the three-yearly health check on the scheme — found the fund had enough assets to cover all pensions and still hold a surplus of £301m. In 2022 the fund was 97 per cent funded; it is now 119 per cent funded. This improvement prompted the lower contributions.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 3. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26

findings.headline: Employer primary contribution rate set at 17.4% for 2026-29 following 2025 actuarial valuation
findings.detail: The council's employer contribution to the pension fund has been set at a primary rate of 17.4% from 1 April 2026 through 31 March 2029, determined by the triennial actuarial review as at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are a material cost on the council's budget; a stable or reducing rate across the three-year period aids financial planning
findings.quote: With effect from 1 April 20 26 to 31 March 20 29, the actuarial review carried out for 31 March 2025 resulted in the Council's employer primary contribution rate being set at 17.4%.

findings.headline: Pension fund membership continues to mature with pensioner numbers growing while contributor numbers remain static
findings.detail: Active members remained stable at 6,737 (2025-26 vs 6,728 prior year) while pensioner numbers grew from 8,996 to 9,338 (+342, +3.8% year-on-year). Deferred members increased to 12,044. The admin team (10.4 FTE) now serves 2,704 members per staff member, up from 2,903 in the prior year, indicating increasing transaction complexity.
findings.matters: A maturing pension fund requires higher annual benefit payments relative to contributions, eventually necessitating asset liquidation rather than cash flow from new contributions. This structural change will increasingly pressure funding, even after the current surplus is achieved.
findings.figures: Pensioners: 9,338 (2025-26) vs 8,996 (2024-25), +3.8%; Active members: 6,737 stable; Deferred: 12,044 stable; Total membership: 28,119; Ratio: 2,704 members per 1 FTE (2025-26) vs 2,903 (2024-25)
findings.quote: the Membership of the Fund continues to mature and amidst a prolonged period of higher inflation, both of which increase the Fund's liabilities

findings.headline: Investment strategy updated to allocate 1-3% of assets to local investment in LCIV pooling area
findings.detail: The revised Investment Strategy Statement (March 2026) introduced a new local investment framework aligned with government policy, setting a target allocation of 1-3% of total fund assets (£20-60m based on current size) for investments in the LCIV pooling area to support sustainable economic development.
findings.matters: Local investment mandates can increase governance complexity and may create conflicts between fiduciary duty (maximum returns) and policy objectives (supporting local economy). This commitment creates future reporting and monitoring obligations and constrains flexibility in asset allocation.
findings.figures: Local investment target: 1-3% of total assets (approximately £20-60m); LCIV pooling area footprint covers 33 London local authorities
findings.quote: A target allocation of between 1-3% of total assets is set aside for this purpose. LCIV will play a central role in identifying, monitoring, and stewarding these investments, ensuring that they deliver both financial returns and broader community benefits.

findings.headline: Pension administration expenses reduced 22.4% to £1.076m year-on-year
findings.detail: Administration expenses fell from £1.387m to £1.076m (down £311k), and total fund expenses (administration, oversight, and investment management) fell 15.0% from £3.870m to £3.287m. Investment management fees rose 10.1% to £1.598m, likely reflecting the transition to LCIV and increased passive fund costs.
findings.matters: Expense reductions improve net returns to the fund. However, the rise in investment management fees may indicate that pooling cost savings have not yet materialised, and per-member administration unit costs remain high at £169 per active member, £27 per deferred, £17 per pensioner.
findings.figures: Admin expenses £1,076k (2025-26) vs £1,387k (2024-25), down 22.4%; Total expenses £3,287k vs £3,870k, down 15.0%; Management fees £1,598k vs £1,452k, up 10.1%

findings.headline: 100% of fund assets transitioned to London CIV pooled arrangements by 31 March 2026 deadline
findings.detail: The council completed its compliance with the government's mandatory asset pooling requirement by moving all assets to the London Collective Investment Vehicle. An Investment Management Agreement was executed delegating implementation responsibility to LCIV while the council retains fiduciary duties including setting strategic asset allocation. This marks completion of a major structural transformation.
findings.matters: Achieving the government pooling deadline on time removes regulatory compliance risk. Pooling was expected to deliver cost efficiencies through scale, though the transition introduced reliance on a single primary manager and some uncertainty around transition costs.
findings.figures: 100% of assets in LCIV by 31 March 2026; 33 London authorities now shareholders in LCIV
findings.quote: By the end of March 2026, the Fund had transitioned 100% of its assets to the London CIV (LCIV), achieving full compliance with national pooling requirements and aligning with the broader policy objective of consolidating LGPS assets into larger, FCA-regulated investment pools.
